author: Kaitlyn McCormick
title: What's 'Freaky Friday?' Camden City School District warns of new potential ICE program - NewsBreak
text:
By Kaitlyn McCormick ,
9 hours ago
Camden City School District officials are warning students and families of a potential new program from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, aka ICE.
The program, called "Freaky Friday," is expected to focus on unaccompanied children 14 and older, whether released or still in custody, according to a letter sent to the school officials from members of the nonprofit Camden Center for Law and Social Justice Inc.
These "Freaky Friday" letters may "use strong or threatening language," offer the receivers $2,500 to return to their home country and warn of parental arrests from noncompliance. They also may state that the receiver will be detained when they turn 18 or ask the receiver to "waive" rights or withdraw their immigration case, according to the nonprofit.
More: Norcross, Conaway say Trump admin still mum on details for Fort Dix migrant detention plan
"Our goal is not to create fear or confusion, but to ensure that we share any information that we receive in a transparent and timely manner," said Acting State District Superintendent Davida Coe-Brockington in an Oct. 5 letter to the district's families and staff.
"We strongly encourage all families to continue sending their children to school each day. School is a safe place where students receive academic instruction, meals, emotional support, and access to trusted adults."
Coe-Brockington said that those receiving a "Freaky Friday" letter still have rights, and encouraged students or parents who may receive a letter to show it to an advocate, lawyer or other trusted adult.
According to information prepared by members of the nonprofit National Immigrant Justice Center & Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, the program appears to affect those who arrived in the U.S. as "unaccompanied children," not all immigrant children.
The operation also doesn't appear to involve threats of ICE arrests or increased ICE presence at schools, shelters or other locations.
Information on the program was obtained from a "widely circulated email, citing trusted sources" sent Oct. 2, the National Immigrant Justice Center press release said.
"This operation appears to pressure certain vulnerable children in federal care, and possibly some young people who were previously detained, to give up their legal rights and applications for humanitarian protection and to agree to depart the United States," the release stated.
More: Sherrill has more cash than Ciattarelli as NJ governor race hits final stretch
In 2020, members of Camden City School District's advisory board approved Resolution 165, reinforcing Camden City School District's commitment to providing a safe and welcoming educational space for students regardless of their immigration status.
Coe-Brockington said that this resolution means district officials don't collect or share immigration status in ways other than legally required, will not assist with immigration enforcement on school campuses unless legally required, and support ICE policies that may restrict enforcement actions in or around schools.
Students or parents with questions were encouraged to contact workers with the district's solution center at 856-966-2507.
An ICE representative was not immediately available to confirm or deny the "Freaky Friday" program's existence.
